A cottage is a small, simple house, usually found in the countryside, a village, by the sea, or near a lake. It is not grand or spacious — it is modest in size, and that modesty is a defining part of what makes it a cottage.

Think of it this way: if you picture a tiny, charming little house tucked into a green hillside, with a small garden, maybe old stone walls or a thatched straw roof, flowers growing near the door — that is the classic image of a cottage.
What Makes Something a "Cottage" and Not Just a "House"?

The word house is a broad, neutral term — it can mean any home of any size. A cottage, however, carries three specific qualities that set it apart:

  1. Small size — A cottage is never large. It usually has only a few rooms. If you walk into one and find yourself in a sprawling, multi-story mansion, someone has used the word very loosely.
  2. Simple or modest design — Cottages are not meant to be grand or impressive. They are practical, unpretentious, and often old-fashioned in style. Many have low ceilings, thick stone or brick walls, small windows, and exposed wooden beams.
  3. Rural or natural setting — Cottages are almost always connected to nature. They sit in villages, on farms, near rivers, by the coast, or in forests. You would not typically call an apartment in a city a cottage.

Beyond its physical description, the word cottage carries a strong emotional atmosphere. It suggests:

  • Coziness and warmth — a place that feels snug and sheltered, especially in contrast to the open landscape around it.
  • Quiet and peace — away from the noise and rush of city life.
  • Old-world charm — something that looks like it belongs to a simpler, older time.
  • Closeness to nature — surrounded by fields, trees, gardens, or water.

When people describe a place as "cottage-like," they mean it feels intimate, homely, and pleasantly old-fashioned — never cold, impersonal, or modern.

1. As a permanent home (historically and still today)
In the past, cottages were the everyday homes of ordinary working people — farmers, fishermen, labourers — who needed a simple, affordable dwelling close to where they worked. Many historic villages in countries like England, Ireland, and Scotland are filled with these original cottages, some of which are still lived in today.

2. As a holiday or vacation home (very common today)
In modern usage — especially in the United Kingdom, Canada, the United States, and Australia — a cottage is often a getaway home that a family uses during holidays or weekends. You might hear someone say, "We're heading up to the cottage this weekend," meaning they are going to a small house they own or have rented, usually near a lake, the sea, or in the mountains. The purpose is relaxation and escape from daily life.

3. As a rental property
Many cottages — particularly in tourist areas like the English countryside, the Scottish Highlands, or lakeside regions in Canada — are rented out to holidaymakers. People book a cottage the way they would book a hotel, but instead of a room, they get an entire small house to themselves for a few days or weeks.
How a Cottage Differs from Similar Words

It helps to understand a cottage by placing it next to other words that describe small shelters:

  • House — a general word for any home of any size, anywhere. A cottage is a specific type of house.
  • Cabin — also small and rural, but a cabin tends to be rougher, more rustic, and often built from logs. It feels more rugged and outdoorsy than a cottage, which feels more charming and homely.
  • Bungalow — a small, single-story house, but typically in a more suburban or residential setting. A bungalow does not carry the rural, old-fashioned charm of a cottage.
  • Hut — even smaller and more primitive than a cottage; usually temporary or very basic in construction.
  • Villa — almost the opposite of a cottage. A villa is large, elegant, and often luxurious, typically found in warm climates.
  • Manor or mansion — large, grand, and impressive. Nothing like a cottage.

So the cottage occupies a very specific space: small, but loveable; simple, but characterful; rural, but comfortable.
Compound Words and Phrases That Use "Cottage"

The word cottage appears in several fixed expressions, each of which borrows the idea of something small-scale and homely:

  • Cottage industry — a small business where work is done at home, or in a very small, informal setup, rather than in a large factory. Example: "Her handmade jewellery business started as a cottage industry."
  • Cottage cheese — a soft, fresh, lumpy white cheese with a mild taste. It is called this because it was traditionally made at home (in a cottage) using leftover milk.
  • Cottage garden — a style of informal, colourful garden filled with a cheerful mix of flowers, herbs, and plants growing closely together, in a way that looks natural and unplanned rather than perfectly manicured. It is the kind of garden you would picture surrounding a traditional country cottage.
  • Cottage pie — a British dish made of minced meat (usually beef) topped with mashed potato and baked. It is "humble" food, home cooking — the kind associated with a simple cottage kitchen.
  • Cottage hospital — a small, local hospital in a rural area, serving the immediate community rather than being a large city facility.

• "They spent their honeymoon in a stone cottage overlooking the sea."
  • "The old couple had lived in the same thatched cottage for fifty years."
  • "We rented a lakeside cottage for a week during the summer holidays."
  • "The painting showed a peaceful cottage surrounded by wildflowers."
  • "She dreamed of leaving the city and retiring to a quiet cottage in the countryside."

A cottage is a small, simply built, charming house — most often set in the countryside, a village, or near water — that is associated with coziness, natural surroundings, and a quiet, old-fashioned way of life, and which is used either as a permanent home or, very commonly today, as a holiday retreat.
